title: Introduction to Python
summary: Learn to write simple Python programs using variables, input, decisions, loops, lists and functions.
audience: Beginners aged 14 and up. No prior coding needed

lessons.title: Your first program: print, variables and types

body.p: Python is a programming language: you write instructions and the computer follows them one line at a time, from top to bottom. You do not need to install anything for this course. Use any Python 3 environment you can reach, such as an online Python interpreter in your browser or Python on a computer. Type each example, run it, and compare what you see with the output shown here.
The print function shows something on the screen. Text goes inside quotation marks and is called a string. Numbers need no quotes, and Python can calculate with them straight away.

A variable is a name that holds a value, like a labelled box. You create one with a single equals sign, which means: store the value on the right in the name on the left. Here a shop sells exercise books at 350 naira each and a customer buys 4.

body.code:
item = "exercise book"
price = 350
quantity = 4
total = price * quantity
print(item)
print(total)

body.p: Because total is calculated from price and quantity, changing quantity to 5 and running again gives 1750 with no other edit. Variable names may use letters, digits and underscores, cannot start with a digit, and are case sensitive, so Price and price are different names. Choose clear names such as exam_score.
Every value has a type. The type function tells you which one Python is using.

list: str is text, such as "Lagos" or "Class 5B".
int is a whole number, such as 350 or -4.
float is a number with a decimal point, such as 12.5.
bool is either True or False, written with a capital first letter.

body.tip: A single equals sign stores a value. Two equals signs compare two values, and you will meet them in lesson 3.

body.p: Programs become useful when they talk to people. The input function pauses the program, shows a question, and waits for the user to type an answer. Whatever is typed comes back as a string, even if it looks like a number. In the examples below, the text after each question is what the user typed.

body.code:
name = input("Your name: ")
price = float(input("Price of one pen in cedis: "))
count = int(input("How many pens? "))
total = price * count
print(f"{name}, your total is {total:.2f} cedis")

Your name: Ama
Price of one pen in cedis: 2.5
How many pens? 6
Ama, your total is 15.00 cedis

body.p: Two new ideas appear here. First, float() and int() convert the typed text into a decimal number or a whole number so that we can multiply. Second, the print line uses an f-string: a string that starts with the letter f. Anything inside curly brackets is replaced by the value of that variable or calculation.
If you forget to convert, Python joins the two pieces of text instead of adding the numbers. Compare these two lines when the user types 4 and then 5.

body.code:
a = input("First number: ")
b = input("Second number: ")
print(a + b)
print(int(a) + int(b))

body.p: The first line prints the text 4 followed by the text 5, which is 45. The second line converts both to whole numbers and adds them to get 9.
After a colon inside the brackets you can control how a number looks. The code .2f means two decimal places, which suits money. A comma adds thousands separators.

body.code:
rent = 45000
price = 19.989
print(f"Rent: {rent:,} shillings")
print(f"Book: {price:.2f} euros")
print("Total:", 15)

list: print can take several items separated by commas and puts a space between them.
{value:.2f} rounds only the display to two decimals.

body.tip: Always wrap input() in int() or float() when you plan to calculate with the answer.

body.p: Python is a powerful calculator. The basic operators are plus, minus, times (written *), divide (written /), floor division (written //), remainder (written %) and power (written **). Floor division gives the whole number of times one number fits into another, and the remainder is what is left over. Suppose a class fund of 1000 dalasi is shared equally among 3 students.

Each student gets 333 dalasi and 1 is left over. Normal division gives a decimal answer. Python follows the usual order of operations, so multiplication happens before addition unless brackets change that.
Comparison operators ask a yes or no question and produce True or False. They are == (equal to), != (not equal to), <, >, <= and >=.

body.h: Making decisions with if, elif and else

body.p: An if statement runs its indented lines only when the condition is True. Use elif for further conditions and else for everything left. Python checks from the top and stops at the first match, so the order matters. The indentation, normally four spaces, is part of the syntax.
A score of 62 is also at least 50, but the elif for 60 comes first, so Grade B is printed. The word and needs both sides to be True; or needs only one.

body.tip: Do not confuse = with ==. One stores a value, the other asks a question.

body.p: A loop repeats instructions so you do not have to write them again and again. A for loop runs once for each value in a sequence. The function range(1, 6) produces the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5: the start is included but the stop value is not. Here is a small times table.

body.code:
for n in range(1, 6):
    print(f"7 x {n} = {7 * n}")

body.p: The indented line is the loop body. It runs five times, and n takes a new value each time. With one number, range(5) starts at 0 and stops before 5. A third number sets the step.
Set a variable before the loop, then add to it each time round. The shorthand total += 200 means total = total + 200. Imagine saving 200 shillings every day for five days.

body.code:
total = 0
for day in range(1, 6):
    total += 200
    print(f"Day {day}: {total}")

body.p: A while loop keeps going as long as its condition is True. Use it when you do not know in advance how many repeats are needed. This program counts how many weeks it takes to save at least 400 pounds at 50 pounds per week.

body.code:
savings = 0
weeks = 0
while savings < 400:
    savings += 50
    weeks += 1
print(f"{weeks} weeks to save {savings} pounds")

body.p: The break statement leaves a loop early. This loop searches for the first whole number whose square is greater than 50.

body.tip: If a while loop never changes the variable in its condition, it runs forever. Stop it with the stop button of your Python environment and fix the condition.

body.p: A list stores several values in order, written inside square brackets. Positions start at 0, so the first item is at position 0 and the last can be reached with -1. Here are five exam scores, and then a sixth is added.

body.code:
scores = [72, 58, 85, 64, 91]
print(len(scores))
print(scores[0])
print(scores[-1])
scores.append(77)
print(scores)
print(sum(scores) / len(scores))
print(max(scores), min(scores))

body.p: The six scores add up to 447, and 447 divided by 6 is 74.5. The functions len, sum, max and min work on any list of numbers. A for loop can visit each item in turn.

A function is a named, reusable block of code. You define it with def, list its parameters in brackets, and send a result back with return. Writing a calculation once and reusing it avoids mistakes. This function adds sales tax, called VAT in some countries, to a price in euros.
Functions can call each other and work with lists. Below, average takes a list of marks and letter turns an average into a grade.

list: return sends a value back so you can store it or use it in a calculation.
print only shows text on the screen. A function without return gives back None.
Parameters are the names in the definition; arguments are the values you pass in.

lessons.title: Reading errors and a mini project

body.p: Every programmer sees errors daily, so learn to read them calmly. When Python cannot continue it prints a traceback. Read it from the bottom: the last line names the kind of error and explains it, and the line above it shows which line of your program failed. Here are the errors beginners meet most. The messages are shown as produced by a recent Python 3; newer versions may add a hint such as Did you mean.

list: A misspelled variable name: NameError: name 'pricee' is not defined
Joining text and a number: TypeError: can only concatenate str (not "int") to str
Converting text that is not a number: ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: 'abc'
Dividing by zero: ZeroDivisionError: division by zero
Using a position that does not exist: IndexError: list index out of range

body.p: A SyntaxError means Python cannot understand the line at all, for example a missing closing bracket or quotation mark. An IndentationError means the spaces at the start of a line are wrong. In both cases the traceback points to the line or just above it.

steps: Read the last line of the traceback and say what it means in your own words.
Find the line number it mentions and read that line slowly.
Check spelling, brackets, quotation marks and indentation.
Change one thing, run again, and read the new message.

body.h: Putting it together: a marks calculator

body.p: This program uses a list, a loop, input, a function and an f-string. The user types three marks and the program prints the average and a grade.

body.code:
Maths mark: 72
English mark: 65
Science mark: 58
Average: 65.0
Grade: B

body.p: The marks 72, 65 and 58 add up to 195, and 195 divided by 3 is 65.0, which falls in the 60 to 69 band and earns a B. Try changing the subjects, the number of marks, or the grade boundaries to match your own school or university scale.

body.tip: Keep practising by changing one thing at a time. Small experiments teach more than copying long programs.
